articles.title: A new chapter in targeting kinase enzymes in cancer
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02776-yInhibitors of tyrosine kinase enzymes have been a cornerstone in precision cancer treatments. Now, targeted protein degraders could reshape therapeutic options.
articles.content:
Targeted therapies have led to striking improvements in outcomes for people who have advanced cancer. Small molecules that inhibit the function of kinase enzymes that have acquired cancer-promoting activity have been particularly effective at treating lung cancer. Twenty-eight kinase inhibitors have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for nine molecular subsets of the disease. Although these inhibitors can result in cancer remission, in some cases lasting years, many people’s cancers eventually return. This is often because the kinase has acquired changes in amino-acid residues at or around the kinase’s active site, causing resistance to the drug. Writing in Nature, Conery et al.1 report an alternative and potentially powerful approach to treating these cancers that eliminates the target kinase rather than just inhibiting its function.

articles.title: Lab-grown brain organoids: time for international oversight
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03048-5Researchers in the field are right to focus on biosafety, ethics and the involvement of patient groups and the public.
articles.content:
Researchers in the field are right to focus on biosafety, ethics and the involvement of patient groups and the public.

A cross-sectional scan of one of the transplanted lab-grown human brain organoids in a mouse, obtained using magnetic resonance imaging. Colours represent the direction of nerve fibres (green, top to bottom; red, front to back; blue, side to side).Credit: S. Pasca lab/Stanford University

For several days in mid-September, neuroscientist and stem-cell biologist Sergiu Pașca became inseparable from his phone. As one of the principal authors on a study by researchers at Stanford University in California reporting the successful transplant of laboratory-grown human brain ‘organoids’ into mice, he was doing many interviews every day.

Read the paper: Developmental xenocortication using human-derived organoids in mice

The mice had been bred so that almost all of their cerebral cortex was missing from their brains. The transplanted lab-grown human tissue survived and developed working connections to the mice’s brains and spinal cords (K. Kaganovsky et al. Nature 658, 430–441; 2026).

It is without doubt a landmark achievement. Animal studies can reveal only so much about the human brain, and options to study live human brain tissue inside a person are limited. Around a decade ago, the creation of organoids — tiny 3D cellular structures grown in the lab that mimic some functions of real organs — changed this. The latest finding, which represents the most extensive integration of human brain cells into an animal so far, opens up further possibilities to understand conditions such as cerebral palsy and autism spectrum disorders in a nervous system, and to test possible interventions.

At the same time, lab-grown organoids are prompting ever deeper ethical questions. Researchers are asking whether the animals receiving implanted brain organoids might gain any human-like properties of consciousness or cognition. How should these characteristics be measured, and what extra oversight should there be for such studies?

Discussions over establishing an international oversight mechanism for brain organoid research are well under way. Such an instrument was recommended in a policy paper published last year (S. P. Pașca et al. Science 390, 574–577; 2025), preceding a conference in late 2025 that Pașca and his colleagues co-organized with Stanford bioethicist Henry Greely. The event was attended by scientists, ethicists, philosophers, policymakers, science communicators and the families of people affected by brain conditions. It was held at the Asilomar conference centre in California, well known for a 1975 meeting of scientists and research funders that discussed the need for safety measures and oversight at the dawn of genetic modification techniques.

Hybrid brains: the ethics of transplanting human neurons into animals

Much has changed in the intervening five decades. Today, life scientists’ research plans must go through various regulatory and ethics processes before any experiments start. These are designed to ensure that experiments involving biological specimens are conducted safely, that consent has been obtained from study participants, including those donating cells, and that animal welfare requirements are met. That said, some of the questions raised by the latest research into brain organoids are not routinely considered.

What form any further oversight should take, and its terms of reference, are still being worked out. A report from the 2025 Asilomar conference, published earlier this month (see go.nature.com/4dvagey), shows that scientists have a strong desire for any oversight mechanism to provide a service to the research community, such as regularly updated and actionable guidance for research groups.

A crucial question is whether an existing organization or research network should take responsibility for oversight or if a new body should be set up. This is important, because the identity of any eventual entity will help to determine whether it commands authority in the research community for its recommendations to be followed. Existing scientific academies and professional societies have such authority. However, most represent discrete disciplines such as stem-cell research or neuroscience, whereas the study of brain organoids includes researchers from these fields and others in the social sciences and humanities.

Independent advice

The ethical arrangements behind Pașca’s latest study also offer a way forward. In addition to various research-ethics and safety requirements, Stanford established an independent group of ethics advisers who reported to the institution. Members were drawn from disciplines in the sciences, social sciences and humanities, as well as from patient groups. These ethics advisers were involved throughout the project, reviewed plans and documentation for the design of experiments and, where necessary, proposed amendments. They were key partners in the research process. Having independent ethics advisers closely involved throughout the life of a research project is the right thing to do. Not every university will have Stanford’s level of resources, but this is where an oversight mechanism could play a valuable part in providing such a service.

Mini models of the human brain are revealing how this complex organ takes shape

During early research into the use of genetic modification in food and agriculture, the field became embroiled in huge public and media controversies in Europe, Africa and the United States. One reason was a perception that scientists were moving too quickly and not consulting enough, amid concerns that risks and harms needed to be better understood before large-scale deployment occurred. It is clear that lessons have been learnt from those times.

A lot is riding on research using brain organoids. For all those who have been diagnosed with brain disorders, and for their families, this work opens up hope for better understanding and, one day, for treatments. It is thus essential that this research is done to the highest standards of safety, minimizing harms and involving a necessarily wide range of stakeholders from science, social science and patient groups.

articles.title: Scientists find new virus behind mysterious tick illness
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a new tick-borne virus in China that causes flu-like illness and may account for previously unexplained cases of fever, fatigue, digestive problems, and low platelet counts. Most patients with ALTNV alone recovered, but coinfections with another dangerous tick-borne virus were linked to more serious complications.
articles.content:
Scientists in China have discovered a previously unknown tick-borne virus that can cause a flu-like illness involving fever, fatigue, gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, and unusual laboratory results.

Researchers led by the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing have named the newly identified orthonairovirus Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV).

The discovery, reported in the New England Journal of Medicine, grew out of efforts to understand why about 30% of patients with symptoms suggestive of Dabie bandavirus (DBV) infection test negative for the tick-borne hemorrhagic fever.

A Search for the Cause of Unexplained Tick Illness

DBV causes severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), a potentially deadly disease found across Asia. The infection has a case-fatality rate of 10% to 30%. Thrombocytopenia refers to an abnormally low level of platelets, the blood cells involved in clotting. The World Health Organization has identified DBV as a priority pathogen for research.

To investigate unexplained cases, researchers collected samples from people who had been bitten by ticks and were treated at sentinel hospitals in regions of China where tick-borne viruses are known to circulate. Using RNA sequencing and viral isolation, the team detected the previously unknown virus.

"The cocirculation of ALTNV and DBV in the same areas, coupled with their shared tick vector, underscores the need for improved differential diagnosis between infections with these viruses in regions where SFTS is endemic."

Genetic analyses placed ALTNV within the orthonairovirus genus in the family Nairoviridae. Its proteins shared less than 80% of their amino acids with those of other species in the genus, supporting its identification as a distinct virus.

Researchers also exposed laboratory cells to human serum containing ALTNV RNA. The virus grew in the cells and was identified as ALTNV using immunofluorescence to detect viral antigens. Electron microscopy revealed features typical of orthonairoviruses, while additional experiments showed that the virus could replicate in several types of cells.

ALTNV Found in More Than 10% of Patients Tested

Among 3,163 patients included in the study, 10.4% tested positive for ALTNV based on the presence of viral RNA or immunoglobulin M antibodies, which can indicate a recent infection.

The proportion was even higher among people who tested negative for DBV. In that group, 15.1% were positive for ALTNV.

Among patients infected only with ALTNV, the most common symptom was fatigue, reported by 84%. Gastrointestinal (GI) problems occurred in 80%, while 38% developed thrombocytopenia. Elevated aminotransferase concentrations were found in 36% (indicating inflammation or injury of the liver or other tissues; 36%). These patients ultimately recovered completely.

Coinfections Were Linked to More Severe Complications

Researchers also identified 38 patients who were infected with both ALTNV and DBV.

Compared with people infected only with DBV, those with both viruses experienced respiratory symptoms more often, affecting 61% compared with 38%. Kidney impairment was also more common in coinfected patients, occurring in 84% compared with 66%.

Seven of the 38 coinfected patients died, representing 18.4% of that group.

Virus Detected in Ticks Across 15 Provinces

The researchers also tested 47,428 ticks collected from 15 provinces. ALTNV RNA was present in 1.3% of them.

The highest prevalence was found in Haemaphysalis longicornis, commonly known as the Asian longhorned tick, with 1.8% testing positive.

Laboratory experiments provided further evidence that this tick species can spread the virus. Researchers showed that H longicornis was capable of transmitting ALTNV to mice.

Because ALTNV and DBV occur in the same regions and can be spread by the same tick vector, the researchers say distinguishing between the two infections could become increasingly important.

"The cocirculation of ALTNV and DBV in the same areas, coupled with their shared tick vector, underscores the need for improved differential diagnosis between infections with these viruses in regions where SFTS is endemic," the authors concluded.

This finding has broad public health implications by improving diagnosis and understanding of tick-borne diseases, potentially leading to better treatment and prevention strategies. The study is detailed and focused on a single important scientific discovery with tangible benefits for disease control and patient outcomes.
articles.personality_title: Scientists discover new tick virus linked to unexplained illnesses in China
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In parts of Asia, many people bitten by ticks get sick with fever, tiredness, stomach problems, and low blood platelets. Some had symptoms like a known dangerous disease called severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), but tests did not find the usual virus (DBV) causing it. Scientists wanted to find out why.

**What happened** – Researchers in China found a new virus carried by ticks, named Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV). Some patients were infected with both ALTNV and the known DBV virus, and those patients had more serious health problems.

**Impact** – This discovery explains many cases of illness that had no clear cause before. Knowing about ALTNV helps doctors better diagnose tick-related diseases and understand how these viruses spread. It also shows that one type of tick can carry both viruses, which is important for preventing infections.

**What's next step** – Scientists and health workers will work on better tests to tell ALTNV and DBV infections apart. This will help doctors give the right treatment faster. Researchers will also study how to stop the virus from spreading and protect people in areas where these ticks live.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new tick virus discovered in China explains many unexplained illnesses and highlights the need for improved diagnosis and prevention of tick-borne diseases.

Los investigadores también estudiarán cómo detener la propagación del virus y proteger a las personas en las zonas donde viven estas garrapatas.

**Frase clave** – Un nuevo virus transmitido por garrapatas descubierto en China explica muchas enfermedades inexplicables y destaca la necesidad de mejorar el diagnóstico y la prevención de enfermedades transmitidas por garrapatas.

articles.title: Why noise is an underestimated health hazard and what to do about it
articles.summary:

The missing piece, for most people, is understanding what counts as too much. Noise is an environmental health hazard that rarely gets treated as one. […]
The post Why noise is an underestimated health hazard and what to do about it first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Most of the damage noise does to your body is preventable, and the tools you need are either free or already in your pocket. The missing piece, for most people, is understanding what counts as too much.

Noise is an environmental health hazard that rarely gets treated as one. With repeated exposure to traffic, construction, loud restaurants, fitness classes, and live events, sounds that once felt jarring start to feel normal. That normalization is the problem, because what feels fine is not always safe, and the health effects of chronic noise exposure go well beyond your ears.

Why noise is more than a hearing problem

Hearing damage is the most visible consequence: loud sounds permanently damage sensory cells in the inner ear, causing hearing loss and tinnitus, the persistent ringing that follows repeated exposure. But the effects reach further than most people expect.

Noise acts as a stressor, activating the autonomic nervous and endocrine systems and affecting heart rate and blood pressure. It disrupts sleep, triggering stress responses without fully waking a person. Over years, those effects build. Long-term traffic noise exposure has been linked to hypertension, coronary artery disease, stroke, and Type 2 diabetes. The World Health Organization sets its environmental noise guidelines lower than workplace standards for this reason, accounting for longer exposure periods and health effects that have nothing to do with hearing.

Your daily noise dose adds up

The risk from noise depends on how loud it is, how long you are exposed, and how close you are to the source. The widely used occupational benchmark is 85 A-weighted decibels (dBA) averaged over an eight-hour workday, and the math shifts quickly above that. For every three-dBA increase, safe exposure time cuts in half. Four hours at 88 dBA burns through the same daily allowance as a full eight hours at 85.

Exposure also accumulates across the whole day, not just in the loudest moments. The commute, a gym class, a loud dinner out, and an evening show all feed the same running total. There is no reset between environments.

Free tools to measure where you stand

The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health offers a free app, the NIOSH Sound Level Meter, that estimates noise levels around you in real time. Most people have no real sense of what their daily exposure looks like. The app gives you a baseline.

Most smartphones also let you set an upper volume limit for audio, which keeps listening levels from creeping up as ambient noise gets louder. Noise-canceling headphones work on the same principle: they cut background noise so the volume you need to hear clearly stays lower.

What you can do right now

Distance from the source is one of the most effective adjustments available. At concerts and sporting events, moving away from speakers makes a measurable difference. During loud tasks at home, fitted earplugs or earmuffs worn from the start protect against damage that builds before noise starts to feel uncomfortable. Filtered earplugs reduce volume without sacrificing clarity, making them practical in social settings where blocking everything out is not what you want.

Smaller changes matter too. A table away from the kitchen or sound system lowers the ambient level in a loud restaurant. Car windows up in heavy traffic reduces exposure on the commute. Battery-powered lawn equipment runs quieter than gas-powered. Appliance noise ratings are in the product specs and easy to compare before buying.

The bigger picture

Individual steps matter, but audiologist Laura Coco, an associate professor at San Diego State University, is direct about the limits: noise pollution will not be solved one pair of earplugs at a time. A farmer cannot turn down the noise on a tractor. A child cannot reroute the highway outside their bedroom. A restaurant worker may spend an entire shift next to a live band with no option to step away.

That is a design problem, a planning problem, and an employer responsibility, and it has to be addressed at those levels: manufacturers building quieter equipment, architects factoring acoustics into buildings, city planners reducing transportation noise. The science on why it matters is done, and the question is whether noise gets treated with the same seriousness as the other environmental hazards it belongs alongside.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.personality_title: Understanding and reducing the hidden health risks of noise
articles.personality_presentation:

**What happened** – Experts explain that loud noise can damage hearing permanently and also cause stress, raise blood pressure, and disrupt sleep. These effects can lead to serious illnesses like heart disease and diabetes. A government app helps people measure noise levels around them. Simple actions like moving away from loud sounds, using earplugs, or choosing quieter appliances can lower noise exposure.

**Impact** – This is important because noise harm adds up throughout the day, not just in the loudest moments. Most people don’t know when noise becomes unsafe. The article shows easy ways individuals can protect themselves and points out that bigger changes are needed in city planning, building design, and work environments to reduce noise for everyone.

Meanwhile, governments, businesses, and planners need to create quieter spaces and products to protect public health on a wider scale.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Noise is more than just a hearing problem—it quietly harms health in many ways, but simple steps and bigger changes can help protect us all.

articles.personality_title_es: Entender y reducir los riesgos ocultos del ruido para la salud
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El ruido está a nuestro alrededor—desde el tráfico hasta los restaurantes ruidosos—pero la mayoría de las personas no sabe cuánto puede dañar su salud con el tiempo. El ruido suele verse solo como un problema de audición, pero afecta mucho más.

**Qué pasó** – Expertos explican que el ruido fuerte puede dañar la audición para siempre, además de causar estrés, aumentar la presión arterial y alterar el sueño. Estos efectos pueden causar enfermedades graves como problemas del corazón y diabetes. Una aplicación del gobierno ayuda a las personas a medir los niveles de ruido a su alrededor. Acciones sencillas como alejarse de sonidos fuertes, usar tapones para los oídos o elegir aparatos más silenciosos pueden reducir la exposición al ruido.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque el daño por ruido se acumula durante todo el día, no solo en los momentos más ruidosos. La mayoría no sabe cuándo el ruido es peligroso. El artículo muestra formas fáciles para protegerse y señala que se necesitan cambios mayores en la planificación urbana, el diseño de edificios y los lugares de trabajo para reducir el ruido para todos.

**Próximo paso** – Las personas pueden comenzar usando herramientas para medir su exposición al ruido y hacer pequeños cambios, como usar tapones para los oídos o elegir equipos más silenciosos. Mientras tanto, gobiernos, empresas y planificadores deben crear espacios y productos más silenciosos para proteger la salud pública a mayor escala.

**Resumen en una frase** – El ruido es más que un problema de audición: afecta la salud de muchas formas, pero con pasos simples y cambios grandes podemos protegernos todos.
